subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Fold, Cut, and Find Lines of Symmetry in Letters

tasks_in_class.description: Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters.
Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?
Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page.

time_bands.activity: Each child folds a sheet of paper in half and then cuts out the letter 'A' without unfolding, then opens it to see the complete shape. The teacher prompts: 'What did the fold do for you?' A quick count round the class collects words — half, mirror, same, fold — that name what happened. The idea of a line of symmetry as the fold line is voiced by the children in their own words before any formal term is offered.

Children work on Let Us Do, p.136 ("Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters."). They fold square paper and cut each letter, then draw the fold lines on a notebook sketch. Pairs compare which letters needed one fold and which needed two. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How do you know N cannot be cut from a folded sheet?'

Children remain in pairs and tackle Let Us Do, p.136 ("Which letters have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have both vertical and horizontal lines of symmetry?"). They sort the letter cards into three groups and record in a two-column table. A brief sharing round surfaces disagreements (e.g. whether 'O' qualifies) and the class reasons together from the fold test.

Children use folded paper to cut out the diya and boat from Let Us Do, p.136 ("Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page."). They hold up the unfolded cutout and identify the fold line as the line of symmetry. The teacher closes by asking: 'Can every shape be cut this way? What must be true about the shape?'

periods.teacher_notes: Children have encountered lines of symmetry in Grade 4; this unit builds directly on that experience — folding paper to cut letters is the concrete act that makes the abstraction visible again. A common error is assuming every letter has at least one line of symmetry; N and Z often trip children who try to fold and cut them without first thinking. Encourage the fold-test as a reliable check before scissors are lifted.
materials: Square sheets of paper (several per child)
Notebook or plain paper for sketching

section_titles: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
periods.activity_title: Build a Firki, Then Read Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
tasks_in_class.description: Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
tasks_in_class.description: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?
Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter.

homework.description: Find symmetry in digits 1–9 and 0: which have reflection symmetry? Which have rotational symmetry? Which have both?

time_bands.activity: Each child follows the nine-step making sequence at Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137 ("Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw."). The teacher demonstrates the diagonal folds and the stopping-halfway cut step by step. Children pin their firki onto a straw or stick and give it a gentle spin to see the blades turn.

Each child marks a dot on one blade of their firki, then slowly turns it at Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137 ("Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?"). Children record Yes or No in their notebooks for each fractional turn. The teacher asks: 'After how many quarter-turns does the firki first look the same?' — introducing the idea that rotational symmetry means the shape matches itself before a full turn is complete.

Children use their letter cut-outs and tracing paper on Let Us Do, p.138 ("Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter."). They trace each letter, rotate the tracing, and tick which fractional turns give a match. Pairs compare tables and discuss whether H and X behave the same way. The teacher introduces the term 'rotational symmetry' as the name for what the firki and these letters share.

periods.teacher_notes: The firki-making is the concrete anchor for rotational symmetry: the dot observation translates directly into the table children fill for letters. A frequent error is marking ¾-turn as 'same' for a letter that only matches at ½-turn — encourage children to re-trace and check each step rather than assuming that if ½ works, ¾ must too. Digits T-7 (p.138) are set as a home task because in-class time is full; children can use the same tracing-paper method they practised with letters.

section_titles: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
periods.activity_title: Digits, Multi-Digit Numbers, and Symmetry — Reasoning Through Combinations

tasks_in_class.description: Do the numbers 11 and 1001 have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both symmetries?
Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both.

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by collecting the digit findings children brought from the home task (T-7) — a quick class survey: hands up for digits that have only reflection symmetry, only rotational symmetry, or both. Agreements and disagreements are noted on the board. Children refer to their tracing-paper checks to settle disputes, using the same method they applied to letters in the previous unit.

Children investigate Let Us Do, p.138 ("Do the numbers 11 and 1001 have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both symmetries?"). The teacher models: to check rotational symmetry in '11', consider each digit's rotational symmetry and whether the digit order reverses correctly after a half-turn. Children then write their reasoning in words. Pairs share before the class settles on an answer.

Children work on Let Us Do, p.138 ("Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both."). This is an unhurried reasoning activity: children propose numbers, apply the digit-level symmetry checks they built, and justify why their number qualifies. The teacher asks a few groups to share one example each and explain their reasoning; the class votes agree or disagree.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have worked through the digit classification find that combining digit symmetry into number symmetry is the harder reasoning step — the most common error is forgetting that a half-turn reverses the order of digits, so '16' turned upside-down reads '91', not '16'. Prompt children to physically write the digits, rotate the paper, and re-read rather than working purely in their heads. The open-ended example-finding task (T-9) naturally stretches children who finish quickly: ask them to find a 4-digit example that has both symmetry types.

section_titles: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
periods.activity_title: Create and Modify Designs to Satisfy Symmetry Conditions

tasks_in_class.description: Does the given cross-shaped design (circle with four directional triangles) have rotational symmetry? Yes/No.
Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.
Modify or add more shapes so the new design looks the same after ¼ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.
Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?
Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?

homework.description: Cut out squares and equilateral triangles (same side length, from end of book) and make different symmetrical designs using these two shapes.

time_bands.activity: Children examine the cross-shaped design at Making Designs (a), p.139 ("Does the given cross-shaped design (circle with four directional triangles) have rotational symmetry? Yes/No."). They trace it, rotate the tracing by a quarter-turn, and note whether it matches. The class discusses which fractional turns give a match, using the fractional-turn language built through the firki and letter work.

Children draw the cross design in their notebooks and tackle Making Designs (b), p.139 ("Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.") and Making Designs (c), p.139 ("Modify or add more shapes so the new design looks the same after ¼ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook."). They work individually, then share with a neighbour to check by rotating the neighbour's notebook. The teacher prompts: 'For ¼ turn, how many times must your added shape appear around the centre?'

Children look at the 2-colour 2×2 grid in Let Us Think, p.139 ("Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?"). They reason through each fractional turn and record. The teacher asks: 'Could you recolour the squares to make ¼-turn symmetry work?', leading naturally into the star-grid task.

Children work on the star-grid colouring task at Let Us Think, p.139 ("Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?"). This is an unhurried making activity; children who finish early are invited to count exactly how many positions in one full turn give a match and write a sentence explaining why.

periods.teacher_notes: The reasoning about reflection symmetry in the modified designs (T-13, p.139) is closely related to T-12 and T-17; additional practice on those is noted for reference: Making Designs (d) and Let Us Do Q17, p.139, may be assigned as classwork or set alongside the cut-shape homework. A common error when modifying the cross for half-turn symmetry is adding a shape on one side only — remind children that the shape must appear on both opposite sides for the half-turn to produce a match.
materials: Coloured pencils or crayons (at least two colours)

section_titles: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
periods.activity_title: Block Printing Craft — Matching Blocks to Prints and Classifying Border Designs

tasks_in_class.description: Does the composite shape (two triangles flanking a 2×2 square) have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn? Does it have both?
Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you.
Observe shapes on the border of the page. Put a ✓ on shapes with reflection symmetry. Put a * on shapes with rotational symmetry.
Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'
Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly describes Rajasthan block printing — a wooden block carved with a design is pressed on fabric repeatedly to make a pattern. Children examine the composite shape (triangles flanking a 2×2 square) at Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Does the composite shape (two triangles flanking a 2×2 square) have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn? Does it have both?"). They draw lines of symmetry and discuss which fractional turn gives a match.

Children sort designs in Let Us Explore, p.140 and work on the block-to-print matching task at Let Us Explore, p.140 ("Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you."). The teacher asks: 'When you press a block on paper, what happens to the left and right sides of the design?' — guiding children to see that printing produces a mirror image, connecting mirror reversal to reflection symmetry.

Children work on the border shapes at Let Us Do, p.141 ("Observe shapes on the border of the page. Put a ✓ on shapes with reflection symmetry. Put a * on shapes with rotational symmetry.") and the Design B sentence-completion task at Let Us Do, p.141 ("Design B: fill in 'The design B looks the same after every __ turn. This design has __ symmetry.'"). Pairs check each other's ticks and stars by applying the fold-test and the tracing-rotation test.

Children dip cut okra or potato halves in ink or paint and stamp them on paper in an arrangement that produces a symmetrical pattern, following Project Work, p.141 ("Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown."). After stamping, they identify and label any lines of symmetry or the fractional turn at which the pattern repeats, applying the full vocabulary of the chapter to their own handmade design.

periods.teacher_notes: The block-printing context clarifies a frequent confusion: a wooden block that is not itself symmetric can still produce a symmetric printed pattern when stamped multiple times in a planned arrangement — the symmetry belongs to the arrangement, not the block alone. T-19 (Let Us Explore, p.140 — sorting designs into three symmetry categories) is closely related to T-18 and T-21; it may be used as additional classwork or discussed during the border-shapes segment if time allows.
materials: Ink pads or poster paint on a tray
Tracing paper and pencils for symmetry checks

items.prompt: Fold a square sheet of paper in half once. Without unfolding it, cut out a shape so that when you open the paper you get a complete leaf. Draw the shape you cut and mark the line of symmetry on the opened leaf.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child cuts a half-leaf shape along the folded edge (or free edge); when unfolded the two halves mirror each other. The fold line is the line of symmetry, drawn as a dotted or solid line down the centre of the leaf.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the paper so the fold line becomes the line of symmetry; cut only one half of the shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold and cut freely, then just ask them to point to the fold line; stretch: ask them to cut a shape that has two lines of symmetry using two folds.

exercise.description: Use lines of symmetry to make paper cutouts of diya, boat, and other designs shown on the border of the page.

items.section_title: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
items.prompt: A child marks a small star on one blade of a windmill firki that has four equal blades. She slowly turns the firki. After which turn does the firki first look exactly the same as it did at the start?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After a ¼ turn. A four-bladed firki has four-fold rotational symmetry, so it first matches itself after one quarter of a full turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the equal blades: a firki with four equal blades first matches after 1 ÷ 4 = ¼ turn.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child recognises that the firki has symmetry but thinks in halves, perhaps confusing it with a two-bladed shape.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may be guessing the last fractional turn before a full turn rather than reasoning from the number of blades.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child does not yet understand rotational symmetry — believing a shape only looks the same after a complete rotation.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically turn a cut-out firki and mark when it first looks the same; stretch: ask how many times it looks the same during one full turn and why.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
exercise.description: Follow the nine steps to make your own windmill firki using a square paper, scissors, and a pin on a stick or straw.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: Draw a simple design in your notebook that looks the same after a ½ turn but does NOT look the same after a ¼ turn. Explain in one sentence how you made sure it works for ½ turn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any design with two-fold rotational symmetry (e.g. two identical shapes placed on opposite sides of a centre point, or a letter S). The explanation should say that the same shape appears twice on opposite sides of the centre, so a half-turn brings one onto the other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place a motif and its copy on opposite sides of a central point so a ½ turn maps each onto the other.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a cross-shaped starting design and ask them to add one pair of identical shapes on opposite sides; stretch: ask them to also check whether their design has any lines of reflection symmetry.

exercise.description: Change the design by adding shapes so the new design looks the same after a ½ turn. Draw the new design in your notebook.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: Priya colours a 2×2 square grid using two colours. Her design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does her design look the same during one full turn (not counting the starting position)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 times. If a design looks the same after every ¼ turn, it matches at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns — four positions in total during one full rotation.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A ¼-turn symmetry means the design repeats every 90°; one full turn of 360° contains four such steps.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child counts only the ½-turn and full-turn positions, thinking in halves rather than quarters.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be subtracting one from four (perhaps excluding the full turn but then miscounting the rest).
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child thinks a design looks the same only at the full turn, not understanding the meaning of rotational symmetry at fractional turns.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to count on fingers — quarter, half, three-quarter, full — tapping each; stretch: ask what fraction of a turn gives each match and list all four as fractions.

exercise.description: Colour the given star-grid square using two colours so the design looks the same after every ¼ turn. How many times does the shape look the same during a full turn?

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: Ravi cuts an okra in half and uses it as a printing block. He presses it four times around a centre point, turning it by a ¼ turn each time. Will the final printed pattern have rotational symmetry? Write yes or no and give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. Stamping the same block four times at equal ¼-turn positions means the pattern looks the same after every ¼ turn, giving it four-fold rotational symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each stamp is the same shape placed at equal angular intervals, so the arrangement repeats every ¼ turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to draw four identical shapes around a point (like clock positions 3, 6, 9, 12) and rotate the drawing to check; stretch: ask whether the pattern also has reflection symmetry and how many lines.

exercise.description: Create symmetrical patterns and designs using vegetable blocks (okra, potato). Some examples are shown.

items.prompt: Which of the following letters can be cut from a single sheet of paper folded TWICE (once vertically and once horizontally), meaning it has both a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: X. The letter X has both a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry, so folding the paper twice (once along each axis) lets you cut it from a quarter of the sheet.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each letter with a vertical fold and then a horizontal fold — only X matches itself on both folds.

what_each_option_reveals.A: N has no line of symmetry at all; the child may be confusing rotational symmetry (which N lacks too) with reflection symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.B: E has only a horizontal line of symmetry; the child may not have checked the vertical fold.
what_each_option_reveals.D: V has only a vertical line of symmetry; the child may not have checked the horizontal fold.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child cut-out letters to physically fold and see whether the halves match; stretch: ask them to list all letters from A–Z that have both lines of symmetry.

exercise.description: Which of the alphabet cutouts E N X T K V O can be made by drawing half or quarter of the letter? Draw lines of symmetry on the letters.

items.section_title: Making a Windmill Firki — Rotational Symmetry Introduced
items.prompt: A firki has four equal blades. Arjun marks a dot on one blade and turns the firki slowly. He says: 'The firki looks the same at ¼ turn, ½ turn, ¾ turn, and full turn.' Is Arjun correct? Write yes or no and explain why in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Arjun is correct. A four-bladed firki with equal blades returns to a matching position every ¼ turn, so it looks the same at all four fractional positions he listed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A firki with four equal blades has four-fold rotational symmetry and matches itself at every multiple of ¼ turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to draw four blade positions and mark which one the dot lands on after each quarter-turn; stretch: ask what would change if one blade were made longer — would it still look the same at ¼ turn?

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make a Windmill Firki, p.137
exercise.description: Observe the dot in the firki. Does the firki look the same after ¼, ½, ¾, and a full turn?

items.prompt: Which of the following letters looks the same after a ½ turn but NOT after a ¼ turn?

options.label: D
options.text: None — all four letters look the same after a ¼ turn

teacher_guide.inclusivity: [Verification failed] Refer to the book task anchored to S3.

exercise.description: Observe letters H, I, X, Y at ¼, ½, ¾, and full turns; complete the rotational symmetry table for each letter.

items.section_title: Rotational Symmetry in Letters and Digits
items.prompt: Meera wants to write a 2-digit number that looks the same when she turns her notebook upside-down (a ½ turn). She writes 11. Does 11 have rotational symmetry? Explain your reasoning in two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, 11 has rotational symmetry. The digit 1 has rotational symmetry (it looks the same after a ½ turn), and when the number 11 is turned upside-down the order of digits reverses — but since both digits are 1, the number still reads 11.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether each digit has rotational symmetry, then check whether reversing the digit order (as a ½ turn does) changes the number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write '11' on paper, turn it upside-down, and read it; stretch: ask them to write a 3-digit number with the same property and explain why it works.

exercise.description: Give examples of 2-, 3-, and 4-digit numbers that have rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, or both.

items.section_title: Making Designs with Rotational and Reflection Symmetry
items.prompt: A 2×2 square grid is coloured using two colours: the top-left and bottom-right squares are red; the top-right and bottom-left squares are blue. Does this design look the same after a ½ turn?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the red and blue squares swap positions and produce the same pattern

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the colours move to different corners

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only after a ¼ turn, not a ½ turn

options.label: D
options.text: No, because a 2×2 grid can never have rotational symmetry

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. After a ½ turn the top-left (red) moves to bottom-right and the top-right (blue) moves to bottom-left — both positions are already the same colour, so the pattern looks identical.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the grid, rotate the tracing 180°, and check whether each cell's colour matches the original grid.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child notices that squares move but does not check whether the colour at the new position matches — conflating movement with change.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confuses ¼-turn and ½-turn symmetry; this design does not have ¼-turn symmetry because after 90° the colours do not align.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child holds a misconception that small grids cannot have rotational symmetry, perhaps because they have not yet tested one.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to colour a 2×2 grid on paper, cut it out, and physically rotate it to check; stretch: ask whether the design also has reflection symmetry and to draw any lines of symmetry.

exercise.description: Does the 2-colour 2×2 square design look the same after ½ turn? Does it look the same after ¼ turn?

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: A rectangular shape (longer than it is tall) flanked on each short side by a small triangle is used as a block-print design. Does this composite shape have a vertical line of reflection symmetry, a horizontal line of reflection symmetry, or both? Write your answer and give one reason for each line you claim.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The composite shape has both a vertical and a horizontal line of reflection symmetry. Vertically: the left half mirrors the right half because the rectangle and both triangles are centred on the vertical midline. Horizontally: the top half mirrors the bottom half because the rectangle and triangles are symmetric about the horizontal midline.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the shape along the vertical midline and check for a match; then fold along the horizontal midline and check again.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to trace the shape, fold the tracing along one axis, and see whether the halves align; stretch: ask whether the composite shape also has rotational symmetry and at which fractional turn.

exercise.description: Does the composite shape (two triangles flanking a 2×2 square) have reflection symmetry? Draw lines. Does it have rotational symmetry? At which turn? Does it have both?

items.section_title: Block Printing — Symmetry in Cultural Context
items.prompt: When a wooden block is pressed on fabric to make a print, the print is a mirror image of the block. A block has the letter 'b' carved on it. What letter will appear on the fabric after printing?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: d. Pressing the block on fabric creates a left-right reflection of the carved image; the mirror image of 'b' flipped horizontally is 'd'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reflect the letter 'b' across a vertical axis (left-right flip) to get its mirror image.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child thinks printing reproduces the block exactly without a mirror flip — not yet aware of the reversal that printing causes.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child reflects the letter top-to-bottom rather than left-to-right, producing 'p' instead of 'd'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child applies both a horizontal and vertical flip simultaneously (rotating 180°), producing 'q', confusing rotation with reflection.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write 'b' on paper with a marker, then press another sheet on top and rub to transfer the ink — observe the result; stretch: ask which letters on a block would print the same letter on fabric (letters with a vertical line of symmetry).

exercise.description: Match each wooden block (i–v) to its correct print (a–e) by drawing a line. One is done for you.
